Germany: Germany launched the Second World War on September 1, 1939, and by 1942 its forces occupied most of continental Europe. The Third Reich collapsed in April-May 1945 under Soviet assault from the east and Allied pressure from the west, ending with Hitler's suicide in the Berlin bunker and unconditional surrender on May 8.
France: France fell to Germany in just six weeks in May-June 1940, leading to four years of occupation, collaboration, and resistance. The country was liberated between June and September 1944 following the D-Day landings in Normandy and Operation Dragoon in the south — battles that define more WWII cinema than almost any other theatre.
Poland: Poland was the first country invaded by Germany in September 1939 and among the last to be liberated in 1945. It suffered the highest proportional death toll of any nation in the war — around 17 percent of its pre-war population — and was home to the majority of the Nazi extermination camps, making it the epicentre of the Holocaust.
United Kingdom: Britain stood alone against Nazi Germany from June 1940 to June 1941, surviving the Battle of Britain, the Blitz, and the U-boat siege of the Atlantic. As the arsenal, airfield, and launching pad of Allied operations in Europe, Britain was the indispensable partner without which D-Day and the liberation of Western Europe could not have happened.
Netherlands: The Netherlands was occupied by Germany from May 1940 to May 1945 — five years that included the starvation of the Hunger Winter of 1944-45, the deportation of 75 percent of its Jewish population (the highest proportion in Western Europe), and the failed liberation attempt at Arnhem. The Dutch resistance and those who sheltered Jews are at the heart of some of WWII's most important stories.
Japan: Japan's empire stretched across the Pacific and East Asia by 1942, built on a campaign of conquest that began in Manchuria in 1931 and accelerated with the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941. Japan surrendered in August 1945 following the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki — the only use of nuclear weapons in warfare.
United States: The United States entered the war after Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941 and became the decisive industrial and military power of the Allied coalition. From the Pacific island-hopping campaign to D-Day to the skies over Germany, American forces fought on every front while the home front produced the ships, planes, and weapons that supplied the entire Allied war effort.
Russia: The Soviet Union bore the greatest military and civilian losses of any nation in the war — an estimated 27 million dead. The Eastern Front, stretching from the Arctic to the Black Sea, was the largest and most brutal land campaign in history, including the Siege of Leningrad, the Battle of Stalingrad, and the destruction of Army Group Centre in Operation Bagration.
Norway: Norway was invaded by Germany on April 9, 1940 and occupied for five years. The Norwegian resistance — one of the most active in occupied Europe — carried out sabotage operations including the destruction of the Norsk Hydro heavy water plant at Vemork, denying Germany a key component for a potential atomic weapon.
Italy: Italy fought alongside Germany as an Axis power until September 1943, when it signed an armistice and was subsequently invaded from the south by Allied forces. The Italian campaign then became one of the war's most grinding fronts — the Wehrmacht fought a stubborn defensive war up the peninsula all the way to April 1945.
China: China had been at war with Japan since 1937, suffering invasions, occupations, and atrocities including the Nanjing Massacre. The Second Sino-Japanese War merged into WWII after Pearl Harbor, making China a key Allied theatre in which millions died and which shaped the post-war order across East Asia.
Thailand: Thailand formally allied with Japan in December 1941, allowing Japanese forces to use it as a staging ground for the invasion of Malaya and Burma. The Burma-Thailand Railway — built by Allied POWs and Asian labourers under brutal conditions — passed through this territory, and it is the backdrop for some of WWII's darkest stories of captivity.
Belarus: Belarus was at the heart of some of the most savage fighting and war crimes of the Eastern Front. German forces killed approximately 25 percent of the pre-war population through combat, starvation, reprisal massacres, and the Holocaust. Come and See, set in Belarus, is widely considered the greatest anti-war film ever made.
Czech Republic: Czechoslovakia was the first country dismembered by Hitler's expansionism — first the Sudetenland in 1938, then the remaining Czech lands as the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia in 1939. Prague was the base of Reinhard Heydrich, the Reich Protector assassinated by Czech and Slovak paratroopers in Operation Anthropoid in 1942.
Libya: Libya was the principal battleground of the North African campaign from 1940 to 1943. The shifting front across the Western Desert — Tobruk, El Alamein, Benghazi — defined the reputations of Rommel, Montgomery, and Patton, and shaped the Allied strategy that would eventually lead to the invasion of Italy.
Belgium: Belgium was occupied by Germany from May 1940 to September 1944. The country was the scene of the Battle of the Bulge in December 1944-January 1945 — Hitler's last major offensive in the west, which inflicted some of the heaviest American casualties of the entire war, particularly around Bastogne.
Denmark: Denmark was occupied by Germany from April 9, 1940 — the same day as Norway — in an invasion that took less than six hours. Unlike most occupied countries, Denmark initially retained a degree of autonomy, but in 1943 the Germans dissolved the Danish government. Remarkably, 95 percent of Denmark's Jewish population was evacuated to neutral Sweden by Danish civilians in October 1943.
Pacific Ocean: The Pacific Ocean was the defining theatre of the war between the United States and Japan, fought across thousands of miles of open water and island chains from Hawaii to the Philippine Sea. The battles of Midway, Leyte Gulf, and the island-hopping campaign towards Japan itself determined the outcome of the Pacific War.
Ukraine: Ukraine was devastated by both German invasion and Soviet rule during the war. The Wehrmacht's advance in 1941 was among the fastest in military history, trapping and destroying entire Soviet armies. The Holocaust was brutally implemented across Ukraine — most infamously at Babi Yar near Kyiv, where over 33,000 Jews were shot in two days in September 1941.
International waters: The oceans were a war in themselves — U-boats hunted Allied convoys across the Atlantic, warships fought surface battles in every sea, and the struggle to keep supply lines open consumed enormous resources on both sides. The Battle of the Atlantic was the longest continuous campaign of the war, lasting from September 1939 to May 1945.
Austria: Austria was absorbed into the Third Reich by the Anschluss in March 1938, its population largely welcoming the union. It was a significant provider of manpower and resources to the German war machine. After liberation in 1945, Austria successfully cultivated the myth of being Hitler's first victim rather than a willing participant — a narrative that shaped its politics for decades.
Tunisia: Tunisia became the final battleground of the North African campaign in late 1942 and early 1943, as Allied forces caught the Axis between the Anglo-American force from the west and Montgomery's Eighth Army from the east. The Tunisian campaign ended in May 1943 with the surrender of 250,000 Axis troops — a defeat comparable to Stalingrad.
Greece: Greece was invaded by Italy in October 1940 and by Germany in April 1941. The subsequent occupation was brutal: famine killed an estimated 100,000 Greeks in Athens alone in the winter of 1941-42. Greece was the scene of fierce partisan resistance and significant atrocities by both German and Italian occupation forces.
Atlantic Ocean: The Battle of the Atlantic was fought between U-boat wolf packs and Allied convoy escorts from the first day to the last day of the war. German submarines sank millions of tons of Allied shipping, threatening to strangle Britain. The eventual Allied victory — through codebreaking, air cover, and radar — was as decisive as any land battle.
Finland: Finland fought two wars against the Soviet Union during WWII: the Winter War of 1939-40, in which Finnish forces inflicted devastating casualties on the Red Army before being forced to cede territory, and the Continuation War of 1941-44, fought alongside Germany to retake the lost land. Finland's resistance defined its national identity.
Indonesia: The Dutch East Indies — modern Indonesia — was occupied by Japan from March 1942, ending centuries of Dutch colonial rule. Allied POWs were interned under brutal conditions in camps across Java and Sumatra, and the occupation reshaped the post-war order, fuelling Indonesian independence after Japan's surrender.
Egypt: Egypt, though nominally independent, was the vital base for Britain's Middle East operations. The Western Desert campaign culminated at El Alamein, just 100km from Alexandria, where Montgomery's Eighth Army defeated Rommel in October-November 1942 — the battle Churchill called the turning point, after which 'there were no more victories' for Germany.
Solomon Islands: The Solomons were the scene of some of the fiercest fighting of the Pacific War, beginning with the Guadalcanal campaign of August 1942-February 1943 — the first major American offensive against Japan. The battle cost both sides dearly and marked the turning point after which Japan began its long retreat across the Pacific.
Hungary: Hungary was a German ally until October 1944, when the Arrow Cross fascist party seized power with German support. The final months of the occupation saw the deportation and murder of hundreds of thousands of Hungarian Jews — the last mass deportation of the Holocaust — as Soviet forces closed in from the east.
Australia: Australia contributed forces to every Allied theatre from North Africa to the Pacific, while facing the real prospect of Japanese invasion after the fall of Singapore in February 1942. Darwin was bombed by the same Japanese force that attacked Pearl Harbor, and Japanese submarines entered Sydney Harbour. The Pacific War reshaped Australia's security outlook permanently.
Argentina: Argentina maintained official neutrality throughout most of WWII but became a haven for Nazi war criminals after the defeat of Germany. Adolf Eichmann lived under a false identity near Buenos Aires from 1950 until his capture by the Mossad in 1960 — the basis of Operation Finale.
Mongolia: Mongolia, then a Soviet satellite state, saw some of the early war's most significant engagements in the form of the Battles of Khalkhin Gol against Japan in 1939 — a decisive Soviet victory that shaped Japan's decision not to attack the USSR from the east in 1941, arguably changing the outcome of the whole war.
Singapore: Singapore — the so-called 'Gibraltar of the East' — fell to Japan on February 15, 1942, in what Churchill called the worst disaster in British military history. Some 85,000 Allied troops surrendered, and thousands of POWs endured brutal captivity. The fall shattered the myth of British imperial invincibility across Asia.
Estonia: Estonia was occupied first by the Soviet Union in 1940, then by Germany in 1941, and again by the Soviet Union in 1944. Estonian men were conscripted into both the German Wehrmacht and the Red Army, sometimes with brothers fighting on opposing sides — the central story of the film 1944.
Spain: Spain remained officially neutral but was ideologically aligned with the Axis, sending the Blue Division of volunteers to fight on the Eastern Front alongside Germany. Spain also served as a vital escape route for Allied POWs, downed airmen, and Jewish refugees fleeing through occupied France via the Pyrenees.
Slovakia: Slovakia was nominally independent under a fascist government that allied with Germany and participated in the invasion of the Soviet Union. Slovak Jews were among the earliest deported to Auschwitz. Two Slovak prisoners — Rudolf Vrba and Alfred Wetzler — escaped in 1944 and compiled the Vrba-Wetzler Report documenting the extermination process.
Papua New Guinea: Papua New Guinea was the scene of savage jungle warfare between Japanese and Allied forces from 1942 to 1945. The Kokoda Track campaign — in which Australian and Papuan troops halted the Japanese advance towards Port Moresby — was one of the most physically punishing campaigns of the entire war.
Marshall Islands: The Marshall Islands were seized by Japan early in the war and later the scene of American amphibious assaults as part of the island-hopping campaign towards Japan. The Kwajalein and Eniwetok atolls were captured in February 1944, giving the Americans a vital forward base for further operations in the Central Pacific.
Bosnia and Herzegovina: During the German and Italian occupation of Yugoslavia, Bosnia was part of the puppet Independent State of Croatia, which implemented its own genocidal policies against Serbs, Jews, and Roma. The Yugoslav Partisans under Tito fought some of their most decisive engagements here, including the Battle of the Neretva in 1943.
Palau: Palau's Peleliu island was the site of one of the Pacific War's most controversial battles in September-November 1944. The Battle of Peleliu — portrayed in The Pacific — cost American forces 9,800 casualties and lasted far longer than expected against fanatical Japanese resistance in fortified coral caves.
Morocco: Morocco — then a French protectorate — was the landing site for the American force during Operation Torch in November 1942. Casablanca's port and airfields were strategic targets. The subsequent Casablanca Conference of January 1943, where Churchill and Roosevelt met, set Allied strategy for the rest of the war.
Equatorial Guinea: Spanish-controlled Fernando Po (now Bioko Island, part of Equatorial Guinea) was a neutral port in the Gulf of Guinea where Axis ships sheltered. In January 1942, British Special Operations Executive operatives carried out Operation Postmaster — stealing a German and Italian vessel from the neutral harbour in a daring midnight raid.
Kiribati: The Gilbert Islands (now Kiribati) were occupied by Japan in December 1941 and recaptured by American forces at the Battle of Tarawa in November 1943 — one of the bloodiest 76 hours in Marine Corps history, with nearly 1,000 Americans killed storming a tiny atoll defended by 4,500 Japanese.
Philippines: The Philippines fell to Japan in May 1942 after a brutal campaign including the Bataan Death March. MacArthur's famous promise — 'I shall return' — was fulfilled with the liberation of the islands in 1944-45, involving the Battle of Leyte Gulf, the largest naval battle in history.
Romania: Romania was a German ally from 1940, providing vital oil from the Ploesti fields that fuelled the German war machine. American B-24 bombers flew the famous low-level Tidal Wave raid against Ploesti in August 1943 at catastrophic cost. Romania switched sides in August 1944 as Soviet forces crossed its borders.
